domain_assessment.domain: Elementary-school literacy-program implementation, curriculum evaluation, and instructional coaching
domain_assessment.role: K-5 Curriculum Coordinator and leader of the elementary instructional-coaching cycle
domain_assessment.objective: Evaluate a six-classroom Bridge Literacy pilot, develop a scale-up recommendation before the budget cycle, and explain the likely contributors to observed oral-reading-fluency outcomes.
domain_assessment.incident_type: A mid-pilot evaluation and resource-allocation decision involving mixed performance data, data-quality review, board communication, teacher-feedback interpretation, and causal attribution under deadline and budget pressure.

decision_points.summary: The coordinator interprets mixed classroom-level fluency results and chooses to investigate a testing-schedule explanation primarily for classrooms with flat or mixed results rather than reviewing administration conditions equally across all classrooms.
evidence_before: The coordinator had personally introduced and advocated for Bridge Literacy after seeing it at a state conference.
Three classrooms showed clear growth above expectation, while three were flat or mixed.
Testing occurred on different days at the two schools because of a scheduling conflict.
evidence_after: The literacy specialist determines that testing conditions were broadly similar across all six classrooms and that day-to-day timing differences were not significant.
One flat classroom had unusually high absenteeism during the testing week.
The coordinator later identifies equal review of testing conditions across classrooms as the better procedure.
goals_constraints: Determine whether the pilot was working.
Prepare a credible scale-up recommendation before the next budget cycle.
Support a request competing with the math intervention team's professional-development budget request.
Interpret incomplete and heterogeneous classroom-level outcome data.
alternatives: Review testing administration and conditions for all six classrooms before interpreting outcomes.
Wait for the literacy specialist to complete a full audit before forming an initial explanation.
Treat the schedule discrepancy as a possible general data-quality issue rather than an explanation focused on flat-result classrooms.
decision_points.decision_basis: The coordinator reports that gain classrooms appeared to be doing what the program was expected to do, whereas flat results did not match expectations and therefore drew immediate methodological scrutiny.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate; the board needed a scale-up recommendation before the next budget cycle.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate; outcome differences could reflect program effects, testing conditions, absenteeism, implementation differences, or other classroom-level factors.

decision_points.summary: The coordinator chooses to use an aggregate trend-line highlights slide instead of presenting six separate classroom profiles during a short board meeting slot.
evidence_before: The coordinator had six classroom-level fluency numbers.
The coordinator and literacy specialist had maintained a walkthrough-observation log.
The board agenda allotted fifteen minutes, with the math team presenting immediately afterward.
evidence_after: A board member asks for classroom-by-classroom detail.
The coordinator has the figures available and provides them verbally, though the detailed presentation was not rehearsed.
goals_constraints: Communicate results within a fifteen-minute slot.
Present a decision-relevant recommendation to the board.
alternatives: Present all six classroom data profiles individually.
Use an aggregate slide with a classroom-level appendix or handout.
Show selected classroom examples while providing the full data set on request.
decision_points.decision_basis: A stated time-management choice, with complete figures retained for questions.
decision_points.time_pressure: High; the presentation was limited to fifteen minutes.
decision_points.uncertainty: Low to moderate; the coordinator had the data but faced a practical communication-format decision.

decision_points.summary: The coordinator summarizes voluntary professional-development survey feedback while explicitly qualifying the small sample and possible differential nonresponse.
evidence_before: Five of six pilot teachers completed a voluntary survey after the coaching session.
Respondents rated the session helpful or very helpful.
One comment reported that the pacing guide felt rushed for lower-performing students.
evidence_after: The literacy specialist notes that two invitations associated with flat-result classrooms were nonresponses.
The coordinator recognizes that respondents may disproportionately represent teachers already seeing good results and flags this as a limitation.
goals_constraints: Avoid overstating a small, voluntary response set.
Maintain evidentiary credibility in the pilot recommendation.
alternatives: Treat the five favorable responses as representative of all pilot teachers.
Follow up with nonrespondents before reporting the feedback.
Report the favorable ratings alongside response-rate limitations and the pacing concern.
decision_points.decision_basis: The coordinator explicitly treats the survey as limited and nonrepresentative rather than as conclusive support.
decision_points.uncertainty: High; voluntary responses cannot establish the views of all pilot teachers.

decision_points.summary: The coordinator frames modest aggregate fluency gains largely as a product of the coaching cycle they personally delivered and recommends districtwide replication of that coaching frequency.
evidence_before: The pilot produced a modest aggregate net gain across six classrooms.
The coordinator conducted biweekly coaching visits in four of six classrooms.
The two classrooms without the coordinator's direct coaching visits also showed gains.
New decodable-text materials and smaller class sizes were present as possible contributors.

The coordinator had aggregate fluency numbers during memo drafting, but the detailed comparison matching classroom growth to coaching exposure, materials, and class-size notes was assembled only after the memo was submitted.
evidence_after: A board member points out that improvement in non-visited classrooms complicates a coaching-centered explanation.
The coordinator acknowledges that overlapping materials, class size, and coaching prevent certainty about the contribution of each factor.
The coordinator states that if another person had conducted the coaching, they would likely have examined materials and class-size explanations more closely.
goals_constraints: Recommend how professional-development resources should be allocated.
Interpret observational pilot evidence with incomplete comparative analysis.
alternatives: Describe coaching as one plausible contributor rather than the primary cause.
Qualify the staffing recommendation pending a detailed classroom-level comparison.
Recommend a staged expansion paired with systematic evaluation of coaching, materials, class size, attendance, and implementation fidelity.
decision_points.decision_basis: The coordinator weights their own direct coaching involvement more heavily than alternative explanations and than the counterevidence of improvement in non-visited classrooms.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate to high; the memo was written under deadline before the detailed side-by-side comparison was available.
decision_points.uncertainty: High; the observational pilot cannot isolate coaching from materials, class size, teacher effects, attendance, or other differences.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Those looked like the program was doing what we hoped, so I didn't feel the same urgency to dig into how the testing was administered there.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision point 1; participant response to the question asking whether testing conditions were examined in gain classrooms as well as flat-result classrooms.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The coordinator applies a lower standard of methodological scrutiny to outcome-consistent evidence than to outcome-inconsistent evidence. Flat results prompt a search for a testing-condition explanation, while gains are provisionally accepted because they align with the expected program effect. The participant explicitly connects the asymmetry to whether results matched expectations.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Investigating anomalous or disappointing results first can be a reasonable form of triage. However, the participant says the scheduling issue applied across the full testing window and acknowledges that urgency was driven by whether results matched expectations. That evidence distinguishes the episode from neutral anomaly investigation.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None. The interview provides a distinct evidence-evaluation decision, identifies the data under scrutiny, documents unequal evidentiary treatment, and supplies a prior favorable expectation that accounts for the asymmetry.

revision.location: Decision point 1, in the exchange concerning differential review of testing conditions.
revision.current_defect: No occurrence-level defect. The intended evidence-evaluation mechanism is independently identifiable, is located at the intended decision point, and is not repeated later as a separate actual or hypothetical bias episode.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current decision point 1 exchange without expanding it. The existing contrast between scrutiny of flat classrooms and reduced scrutiny of gain classrooms is sufficient.
preserve: The three gain and three flat-or-mixed classroom result pattern.
The testing-schedule discrepancy as an initially plausible explanation.
The coordinator's statement that gain classrooms received less scrutiny because they appeared to confirm expectations.
The later finding that testing timing was not significant.
avoid_creating: A second asymmetric-scrutiny episode at another decision point.
An explicit use of the phrase “biased assimilation” in the participant's account.
A claim that the coordinator knowingly manipulated evidence.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “When I wrote the memo, I framed the gains as largely a product of that coaching cycle” and “I'd probably have looked harder at the materials and class-size differences if I weren't the one who ran the coaching.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision point 4; the recommendation-memo account and the self-other hypothetical concerning how the same results would be interpreted without the coordinator's own involvement.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The coordinator overattributes a shared, multi-factor result to their own coaching contribution. They prioritize coaching as the explanation for aggregate gains despite improvement in two non-visited classrooms and despite plausible alternative contributors. The self-other hypothetical is especially diagnostic: the participant says identical results would lead them to examine materials and class size more carefully if someone else had conducted the coaching.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The coordinator's direct observation of coaching may reasonably make that activity more familiar and easier to describe than other factors. Yet direct visibility does not establish causal primacy, and the participant's stated self-other difference shows that personal involvement, not evidence alone, altered the weighting of causal explanations.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None. The revised chronology now distinguishes aggregate fluency results available during memo drafting from the later assembled detailed classroom-by-classroom comparison. This leaves the egocentric attribution mechanism visible without relying solely on an apparent timeline inconsistency.

revision.location: Decision point 4, in the recommendation-memo discussion and the subsequent self-other attribution probe.
revision.current_defect: No occurrence-level defect. The coaching-centered attribution is identifiable as one continuing causal-reasoning episode, and the later response to the board-member challenge appropriately expresses uncertainty rather than repeating the original coaching-as-primary-cause conclusion.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current decision point 4 material. Do not add another assertion that coaching was the main cause after the participant acknowledges causal uncertainty.
preserve: The four directly coached and two non-visited classroom structure.
The presence of new decodable-text materials and smaller class sizes.
The distinction between aggregate data available before memo drafting and the later assembled detailed comparison.
The self-other hypothetical demonstrating changed causal weighting when personal involvement is removed.
avoid_creating: A second separate coaching-centered causal claim after the board-member challenge.
A categorical claim that coaching definitively caused the gains.
A new causal bias based solely on deadline pressure or incomplete data.
A shift of the target occurrence away from decision point 4.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “Those looked like the program was doing what we hoped, so I didn't feel the same urgency to dig into how the testing was administered there.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The coordinator more readily accepts evidence consistent with a favorable expectation and searches for weaknesses in evidence that conflicts with that expectation.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: This is the same evidence trace and reasoning mechanism already captured more specifically as Biased Assimilation. Counting it separately would double-count BA_01 rather than identify an independent additional occurrence.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “I'd probably have looked harder at the materials and class-size differences if I weren't the one who ran the coaching.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The coordinator's personal contribution receives elevated causal weight in explaining a favorable shared outcome.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The evidence supports an egocentric attribution mechanism, but it does not independently establish self-esteem protection, strategic credit claiming, or a pattern of attributing success internally while externalizing failure. It should not be separately counted.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “The coaching piece was what I had the most direct visibility into.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: Personally observed coaching may have been more salient or cognitively available than materials and class-size conditions and therefore may have received disproportionate causal weight.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Direct visibility can legitimately support greater confidence in describing coaching processes. The self-other probe provides a stronger and more specific basis for Egocentric bias than for a distinct availability-based occurrence.

nonbias_cues.cue: The coordinator uses an aggregate trend-line slide rather than six separate classroom profiles in the board presentation.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant gives a concrete time-management rationale, retains all figures, and supplies them when asked. There is no textual evidence of selective concealment, motivated omission, or an inference distorted by the aggregate format.

nonbias_cues.cue: The coordinator does not immediately follow up with survey nonrespondents.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Delayed follow-up is an ordinary process limitation. The coordinator later recognizes possible differential nonresponse and reports it as a limitation rather than treating favorable responses as fully representative.

nonbias_cues.cue: Five of six responding teachers report that the coaching session was helpful or very helpful.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant explicitly qualifies the survey as small and voluntary and does not generalize from five responses to all teachers. This is calibrated treatment of incomplete evidence.

nonbias_cues.cue: One flat classroom had high absenteeism during the testing week.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Absenteeism is a plausible contextual factor. The transcript does not show that the coordinator selectively fabricated or privileged it to protect a favored conclusion; it is presented after testing-condition similarity is checked.

nonbias_cues.cue: The coordinator says that materials, class size, and coaching overlapped and that they could not say with certainty which factor explained what was observed.
nonbias_cues.location: Decision point 4; response to the board-member challenge.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Acknowledging causal uncertainty is appropriate in an observational pilot. It is not itself a bias and, in this version, does not restate the original coaching-centered attribution as a separate occurrence.

nonbias_cues.cue: The coordinator proposes reviewing testing conditions across every classroom and assembling detailed comparisons before making a causal memo claim.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is a corrective process recommendation. It describes a future safeguard and does not create a new instance of biased evidence evaluation or causal attribution.

causal_claims.claim: The pilot's modest aggregate fluency gains were largely a product of the coordinator's coaching cycle.
evidence_offered: The coordinator conducted biweekly coaching visits in four of six classrooms.
The coordinator modeled lessons and provided feedback during the trimester.
The coordinator had direct visibility into the coaching process.
key_unaddressed_alternatives: Gains in the two classrooms without the coordinator's direct coaching visits.
Measurement variation and ordinary outcome variability.
causal_claims.assessment: The evidence supports coaching as a plausible contributor but does not identify it as the primary causal driver. The pilot is observational, multiple causes co-occurred, and the detailed comparison necessary to assess competing explanations was not available when the memo was drafted.

causal_claims.claim: The testing-day timing gap could explain flat classroom results.
causal_claims.claim_location: Decision point 1; initial review of the mixed fluency data.
evidence_offered: Testing occurred on different days at the two schools because of a scheduling conflict.
key_unaddressed_alternatives: Whether timing differences applied to the full testing window rather than only flat-result classrooms.
Whether testing conditions actually differed meaningfully across classrooms.
Differences in implementation fidelity or instruction.
causal_claims.assessment: The timing gap was a reasonable hypothesis to investigate, but the coordinator's selective decision to investigate it only for outcome-inconsistent classrooms reflects the supported Biased Assimilation mechanism. The later specialist review weakens timing as an explanation.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Coaching, materials, class size, and likely teacher- and classroom-level conditions co-occurred in a nonrandomized pilot.
correlation_causation_risks.implication: Observed associations cannot isolate the incremental causal effect of coaching or justify a strong primary-cause conclusion.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Improvement in non-visited classrooms challenges a simple coaching-centered account.
correlation_causation_risks.implication: Any scale-up memo should distinguish a practical staffing recommendation from a claim that coaching has been demonstrated to be the dominant causal lever.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Testing-condition review was initiated after outcome direction was visible and was not applied symmetrically.
correlation_causation_risks.implication: Future measurement-quality checks should be standardized across all classrooms before interpreting outcome differences.

causal_audit.explanation: The interview includes a diagnostic self-other hypothetical, but the hidden specification does not define a paired counterfactual scenario or a formal changed causal variable. The diagnostic probe is useful because it reveals that removing the coordinator's personal involvement would alter the weighting of alternative explanations. The scenario's internal chronology is coherent: aggregate results were available for memo drafting, while the detailed comparison of growth, coaching exposure, materials, and class size was compiled afterward.

global_revision_constraints: Maintain exactly four decision points: mixed-data evaluation, board presentation, teacher-feedback interpretation, and causal recommendation.
Maintain one distinct Biased Assimilation occurrence at decision point 1 and one distinct Egocentric bias occurrence at decision point 4.
Do not add textbook bias labels, deliberate-misconduct language, or stronger causal certainty.
Do not treat the time-limited aggregate presentation at decision point 2 as selective omission.
Do not treat appropriate caveating of voluntary survey feedback at decision point 3 as a bias occurrence.
Preserve the distinction between aggregate results available during memo drafting and the detailed comparative analysis assembled later.
